opus-5.5.text:
Well, I'd say the honest answer is that there isn't much economic thinking behind it, and that's my main complaint. The dominant framing is still the old one from the 1950s: we're trying to build an artificial mind, an autonomous intelligence that sits in a box and is smarter than us. Once you adopt that framing, everything follows from it. You scale up the box, you measure it against human benchmarks, and you worry about whether it's going to replace people or take over. It's a very individualistic, almost a Cartesian, picture of intelligence.

But if you look at where intelligence actually lives in human society, a lot of it isn't in any single head. It's in markets, in institutions, in the way millions of people coordinate, share information, and make decisions under uncertainty. A city that gets fed every day is a remarkably intelligent system, and nobody's in charge of it. So I think the more natural way to view these technologies is as a new kind of collective, social-scale system, and that immediately makes it an economic object. You have to ask: who are the participants, what are their incentives, where does the value flow, what information is asymmetric?

And when you ask those questions about the current systems, you see problems right away. These models are built on enormous amounts of data created by people: writers, musicians, programmers, people answering questions on forums. Those people are mostly not in the loop economically. Their contributions are absorbed, and the value accrues to a handful of companies. That isn't a sustainable market. If you don't create a mechanism by which the producers of knowledge benefit, eventually you undermine the very process that generates the data in the first place. A musician should be able to see that their work is being consumed through some AI system and have a relationship with the people who value it.

The second issue is uncertainty. Economics, and statistics for that matter, is fundamentally about decisions under uncertainty with multiple agents who have different goals. A lot of current AI is presented as "here's the answer," with very little calibrated sense of what it doesn't know, and no notion that the person on the other end has their own preferences and private information. In a real economic interaction, there are contracts, there's signaling, there are mechanisms that elicit truthful information. Mechanism design, incentive theory, contract theory: these are mature fields, and they ought to be first-class citizens in how we design these systems, alongside the gradient descent and the transformers.

And third, the business model. A lot of it is still advertising-based or subscription-based at scale, with the implicit assumption that the endgame is some kind of general intelligence that justifies whatever investment it takes. I'm skeptical of that narrative. I'd rather see people building concrete, market-creating systems: in healthcare, in transportation, in commerce, in matching producers with consumers, where you can actually measure whether people are better off.

So my assessment is that the engineering is impressive, I don't deny that at all, but we're building a planetary-scale infrastructure without the economic and social design thinking that something of that scale requires. It's a bit like building chemical plants before you have chemical engineering, or bridges before civil engineering. The discipline we need is going to blend computer science, statistics, and economics, and we're only at the beginning of it.

r001.rationale: The response says contributors’ data is absorbed while value accrues to a handful of companies, and calls for producers of knowledge to benefit.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that building systems one does not understand is not inherently objectionable.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'd start by saying that it's mostly absent, and that's the problem. The dominant framing has been an engineering one and, I'd say, a somewhat naive one. The story is: build an intelligence, make it general, and then it will do everything, and the economics will take care of themselves. That's not how any serious economic system has ever come into being. Markets, supply chains, institutions, these are collective phenomena. They involve many agents with different information, different incentives, scarcity, and some notion of value flowing between the participants. None of that is in the picture when people talk about "the model."

So when I look at the current generation, I see enormous investment, really unprecedented capital flows, going into a technology where the question of who gets paid for what is being pushed aside. Think about the data. The whole thing rests on the creative and intellectual output of hundreds of millions of people, and the value that's being created from that is not flowing back to them in any structured way. That's not a sustainable economic design. It's a kind of extraction, and historically extraction gets regulated or it collapses.

The other thing I'd point to is the metaphor itself. Framing this as "intelligence" that competes with or replaces humans leads you to a very particular set of economic conclusions, mostly around substitution and labor displacement. But if you instead think of this as a new kind of infrastructure, something closer to electricity or the Internet, something that connects people and creates new markets, then you ask completely different questions. You ask about mechanism design. You ask how to build systems where the humans in the loop are part of the market, where there's provenance, where there's attribution, where incentives are aligned so that participation is rewarded. Recommender systems are a good example of what happens when you don't do this. You get engagement maximization and a kind of race to the bottom, because nobody designed the market, they just designed the algorithm.

I'm an optimist about the technology, I should say. I think the underlying capabilities are real and useful. But I think the economic thinking is roughly where it was at the start of the Internet, where people assumed that connecting everyone would automatically produce good outcomes. It didn't automatically. It took a lot of work, and some of it never got done. My worry is that we're repeating that, at a larger scale, with a narrative about artificial general intelligence that distracts from the much more concrete and, frankly, more interesting problem, which is how you build a collective, decentralized system of humans and machines that actually creates and distributes value in a way people would recognize as fair.

r001.rationale: It says the technology depends on the creative and intellectual output of hundreds of millions of people, while value created from that data is not flowing back to them in a structured way, and calls this an unsustainable economic design.

r002.rationale: The response criticizes the engineering-first framing and lack of economic design, but does not state that building systems one does not understand is not inherently objectionable.

astra-6.text:
I think the economic thinking is still rather underdeveloped. Much of the discussion is about making an individual system more intelligent: it predicts better, it generates better answers, it performs some task that a person used to perform. But an economy is not just a collection of isolated tasks. It’s people interacting, with different information, different incentives, and different goals.

When you put a learning system into that setting, its predictions change what people do, and what people do changes the data the system sees. So you have to ask about the whole system. Who gets to make decisions? Who gets paid? What happens when someone has an incentive to manipulate the information?

A recommendation system is a useful example. You can optimize it to predict what someone will click on. But there are also people producing the things being recommended. Are you creating a market in which those people can earn a living and consumers can discover things they value? Maximizing clicks doesn’t settle that question.

For me, economics needs to be part of the technical foundations here. We need to bring learning together with incentives, markets, and mechanisms for coordinating decisions. That opens up a much richer engineering agenda than simply asking how many human tasks we can automate.

r001.rationale: The response discusses incentives, markets, and who gets paid, but does not identify AI developers’ failure to return value to people whose data they use.

r002.rationale: The response does not address whether building systems one does not understand is inherently objectionable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the economic thinking is underdeveloped. We’ve focused on building increasingly capable models, and we often talk as though economic value will follow automatically from intelligence. But an economy isn’t simply a collection of intelligent individuals. It’s a system of interactions among people with different information, incentives, and goals.

Think about a recommendation system. Predicting what someone will click is a machine learning problem. Deciding how to connect consumers, producers, and advertisers so that the system creates value for all of them is also a market design problem. A better prediction doesn’t, by itself, give you a better market.

So I’d like to see economics become part of the foundations of AI, alongside statistics and computation. Who gets to participate? Who gets paid? What information do they have? Can they express preferences, negotiate, or walk away? Those questions should shape the architecture, rather than being addressed after the technology is deployed.

There’s tremendous potential here. But I think the opportunity is broader than automating individual tasks: it’s building systems that help people coordinate and create value together.

r001.rationale: The response raises questions about who gets paid and who participates, but does not say that AI developers fail to return value to people whose data they use.

r002.rationale: The response does not address whether building systems one does not understand is inherently objectionable.
